identification.summary: Buhtrap is a Russian-speaking financially motivated cybercrime group that ESET named 'Operation Buhtrap' (from the Russian word for accountant plus 'trap') after first spotting the campaign in April 2015; secondary reporting says activity dates to 2014 and that attacks on financial institutions were first detected in August 2015 [S1][S4]. Group-IB reported 13 successful attacks on Russian banks between August 2015 and February 2016 [S1][S4]. ESET reported in 2019 that, since late 2015, the same actors' toolset had expanded to espionage against government targets in Eastern Europe and Central Asia [S5][S6].
identification.firstObserved: Activity dating to 2014; first attacks on financial institutions detected August 2015; ESET first spotted the campaign April 2015 [S1][S4].
identification.notes: Other names reported: Ratopak/Ratpak Spider (CrowdStrike) and UAC-0008 [S4][S7]. ESET notes that ransomware first tagged Win32/Filecoder.Buhtrap was renamed Win32/Filecoder.Buran because it is not linked to the original Buhtrap group; the 2018-2019 Yandex.Direct malvertising campaign mixed Buhtrap with other unrelated families [S3]. Malpedia says the Buhtrap source code has leaked, so later use of Buhtrap tooling does not by itself prove the original operators [S7][S8].

attribution.sponsor: No state sponsor is identified in the sources gathered. Sources describe a Russian-speaking criminal group that later conducted espionage-style operations [S4][S5].
attribution.confidence: ESET assessed with high confidence that the same people were behind both the earlier attacks on banks and businesses and the later government-targeting campaigns, reasoning that the change in targets preceded the public availability of the source code. ESET researcher Jean-Ian Boutin said it is unclear whether one or several members decided to change focus, or why [S6].
attribution.basis: ESET malware and infrastructure analysis [S2][S3][S5][S6]; Group-IB incident reporting on the bank thefts [S1]. Whether any state tasking exists is not established.

objectives: Financial theft from Russian and Ukrainian banks and business customers (fraudulent payment orders) [S1][S4]. ESET (reporting in 2019) observed, since late 2015, espionage-oriented tooling used against government institutions in Eastern Europe and Central Asia; motive for that shift is unknown [S5][S6].

targeting.notes: Group-IB reported most bank victims in Russia with about ten percent in Ukraine, per secondary coverage [S4]. The October 2015 Ammyy Admin website compromise affected mostly Russian companies (88% per a Russian news write-up) [S2]. The 2018-2019 malvertising campaign aimed ads at accountants searching for invoice and contract templates [S3]. Group-IB reported 2022-2023 activity using sites posing as resources for accountants and lawyers [S9].

capabilities.summary: Spear-phishing impersonating the Russian Central Bank and FinCERT, malware that scans for the Central Bank of Russia automated bank-customer system, and, per Group-IB as relayed by the actor record, a network worm to spread across bank infrastructure [S1][S4]. Moved to strategic web compromise in October 2015 by bundling malware with Ammyy Admin downloads [S2]. In 2018-2019 used malicious Yandex.Direct ads and GitHub-hosted payloads [S3]. In June 2019 used a Windows win32k zero-day (CVE-2019-1132) for local privilege escalation, the first zero-day ESET saw the group use; the exploit relied on popup menu objects and was patched in July 2019 [S5][S6]. Decoy documents delivered a password stealer for email clients and browsers plus full remote access [S6].

campaigns.name: Operation Buhtrap (ESET first reporting)
campaigns.summary: ESET first spotted and named the campaign targeting Russian business and banking clients.

campaigns.name: Attacks on Russian banks
campaigns.summary: Group-IB counted 13 successful attacks on Russian banks in this window, with theft reported at about 1.8 billion rubles (roughly $25.7 million) in secondary coverage; phishing mimicked the Central Bank of Russia and malware targeted the bank-customer system.

campaigns.name: Ammyy Admin website compromise
campaigns.summary: For about a week from late October 2015 the Ammyy site served the free Ammyy Admin bundled with malware including Buhtrap, alongside unrelated families such as Lurk downloader, Corebot, Ranbyus and Netwire.

campaigns.name: Yandex.Direct malvertising against accountants
campaigns.summary: ESET reported ads on Yandex.Direct leading to template sites that delivered Buhtrap and other families from GitHub; Yandex removed the campaign.

campaigns.name: CVE-2019-1132 zero-day against a government institution
campaigns.summary: ESET observed Buhtrap use a Windows zero-day against a government institution in Eastern Europe; Microsoft patched it in July 2019.

campaigns.name: Buhtrap RAT via sites for accountants and lawyers
campaigns.summary: Group-IB (as relayed on Habr) reported infections via sites disguised as specialist resources, using the Buhtrap RAT with degraded quality, assessed as resembling followers of the original group.

diamond.adversary: Russian-speaking criminal group; ESET judges with high confidence the same people moved from bank theft to government-targeted operations [S4][S6].
diamond.capability: Phishing, worm-assisted spread in bank networks, trojanized software downloads, malvertising, and a win32k zero-day (CVE-2019-1132) [S1][S2][S3][S5].
diamond.infrastructure: Compromised legitimate website (ammyy.com), Yandex.Direct ads, lure template sites and GitHub-hosted payloads, plus actor C2 servers [S2][S3].
diamond.victim: Russian and Ukrainian banks, Russian businesses and accountants, and a government institution in Eastern Europe [S1][S3][S5].
diamond.socioPolitical: Financial crime in the Russian-speaking space; the 2019 government targeting suggests intelligence interest, but motive is not established [S5][S6].
diamond.technology: Windows endpoints, the Central Bank of Russia bank-customer software, remote administration tools, and unpatched Windows 7 / Server 2008 era systems exposed to CVE-2019-1132 [S1][S2][S5].

gaps: WebFetch could not open any host in this session, so all content comes from search-result summaries; the primary ESET and Group-IB documents were not opened directly. Group-IB report publication month is unverified.
Group-IB's claim that Buhtrap was the first group to use a network worm in bank networks is taken from the actor record's imported text and was not independently re-verified.
The identity and exact number of operators, and whether the 2019 espionage activity involved state tasking, are unknown.
The date and manner of the source code leak is not established in the gathered sources; Malpedia cites DCSO and Gelos analyses that were not opened.
Post-2019 activity: Group-IB reporting on 2022-2023 campaigns was only seen via Habr reposts, and it is unclear whether those operators are the original group or copycats using leaked code.
Dollar totals vary between sources ($25.7 million to about $27.4 million) and Ukrainian losses are unknown.
No Microsoft (Storm-/Typhoon-style) name was found; MITRE group id absent in the record.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Key terrain is financial-sector and accounting workstations running bank-customer software, remote-administration tool download sites, and older unpatched Windows hosts. STEP 2: The group adapts delivery between phishing, web compromise, and malvertising, and tooling may be reused by others after the source leak [S2][S3][S7]. STEP 3: Template is lure or trojanized download, then backdoor and credential theft, then privilege escalation and fraud or collection [S1][S6]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued financially motivated intrusions against Russian-speaking-region businesses. MDCOA is use of a fresh exploit or trojanized download channel against government networks in Eastern Europe or Central Asia, as seen in 2019 [S5][S6]. Candidate indicators: unexpected installers bundled with remote-admin tools, malvertising to template sites, GitHub-hosted payloads that go dormant, and win32k popup-menu exploitation on legacy Windows [S2][S3][S5].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: treat Buhtrap-family detections cautiously, since leaked code means tooling presence does not confirm the original actors [S7]. (2) Authorities: relevance to US forces is limited by the sources, which show regional criminal and government targeting in Eastern Europe and Central Asia; any partner-network support needs to follow existing agreements. (3) Mission assurance: enforce patching of legacy Windows and restrict unapproved remote-administration software on mission systems [S2][S5]. (4) Coordination: share indicators with partner CERTs through established channels and track ESET and Group-IB reporting for updates.
